research_material:
I make a timetable every Sunday and quit by Tuesday
how do you study when your phone is right there

pain_points: Planning systems fail by mid-week (loss of momentum/accountability)
Lack of realistic study strategies that account for phone presence
Difficulty maintaining routines beyond initial setup
Unknown what 'actual studying' looks like when distractions are unavoidable

hooks.text: Your Sunday plan lasted 36 hours. Here's what killed it.
That color-coded timetable? It's already dead. You just don't know it yet.
Why your Tuesday self sabotages Sunday's promises every single week.
90% of college schedules fail within 72 hours. You're not broken.
Your timetable isn't the problem. Your brain's reward system is.
You make the perfect schedule then immediately ignore it. Sound familiar?
Sunday optimism, Tuesday chaos, Wednesday regret. The cycle repeats.
That gorgeous Google Calendar you spent 2 hours designing? Dead.
Plot twist: Your timetable didn't fail. Your system did.
Everyone's schedule dies by Tuesday. But your next one won't.

winner.text: You make the perfect schedule then immediately ignore it. Sound familiar?
winner.reasoning: This hook directly calls out the specific shame-to-recognition moment procrastinators experience—they *know* they do this, making it instantly relatable. The conversational "sound familiar" creates parasocial agreement that hooks engagement, while the contradiction (perfect schedule + immediate failure) mirrors their exact pain point without seeming preachy.

runner_up.text: Your Sunday plan lasted 36 hours. Here's what killed it.
runner_up.reasoning: Strong curiosity gap with specific time anchor (36 hours) that feels empirical enough to be credible while vague enough to pull clicks. The 'here's what killed it' positions the carousel as having real answers, appealing to procrastinators' desire for actual solutions.

script.script:
[HOOK - 0-3 sec]
"You make the perfect schedule then immediately ignore it. Sound familiar?"
[PAUSE 1 sec]

[PROBLEM - 3-7 sec]
"Yeah, because schedules fail when they don't match how your brain actually works. You're not lazy—you're just planning like a robot."
[ON-SCREEN TEXT: "your brain ≠ a spreadsheet"]
[CUT]

[VALUE - 7-15 sec]
"Here's what actually works: stop scheduling tasks. Schedule *energy*. Figure out when you're actually focused, build your real deadlines backward, then give yourself permission to work in chunks that don't suck."
[ON-SCREEN TEXT: "energy > time"]
[PAUSE 0.5 sec]
"That's literally it. No motivation required."
[CUT]

[CTA - 15-17 sec]
"Follow for the full system—I'm breaking down exactly how to build a schedule you'll actually stick to."
[ON-SCREEN TEXT: "@[handle]"]
[PAUSE]
script.viewer_takeaway: Traditional schedules fail because they ignore your natural energy patterns. The fix is scheduling based on when you're actually focused, not clock time—and it removes the willpower problem entirely.

frame_plan.on_screen_text: you make perfect schedules then ignore them

Split screen or transition: left shows rigid spreadsheet/calendar app, right shows person's actual chaotic workflow. Show someone trying to force themselves to work. Slightly exaggerated/comedic tone

Person looking relaxed/focused during their peak hours. Show visual representation of 'focused time' vs 'low energy time' (maybe with brightness/color shifts). Show someone building a schedule backwards on whiteboard or notes

Direct address to camera, slight lean-in or gesture toward handle text. Confident, casual tone. Text appears prominently on screen. Optional: quick flash of follow button or profile preview

Brand logo/handle graphic for final frame

justifications.clarity: Hook lands instantly with relatable question, problem identified by 3-sec mark ('your brain ≠ spreadsheet' is concrete), but 'schedule energy' needs one more visual anchor to crystallize.
justifications.retention: Problem-solution structure keeps attention, but value section (7-15s) is dense with three separate concepts competing for cognitive load—risks losing viewers mid-message.
justifications.save_potential: Core insight ('energy over time') is novel enough to bookmark, and backwards-planning detail gives actionable takeaway worth saving for later reference.
justifications.shareability: Relatable pain point + comedic tone help, but lacks the 'wow' moment or surprising stat that makes people tag friends—feels informative rather than conversation-starting.
justifications.audience_fit: Directly addresses procrastinator's core failure (ignoring schedules) and reframes laziness as planning misalignment, matching target's self-perception perfectly.
justifications.cta_strength: Clear ask ('follow for full system'), but no urgency or scarcity lever; 'full system' promises substance but doesn't explain why they can't get it elsewhere.

weaknesses.issue: Middle section overloads three ideas ('energy over time' + 'backward deadlines' + 'work in chunks') in 8 seconds, forcing viewer to process faster than retention allows.
weaknesses.fix: Split VALUE into two tiers: (7-11s) 'Stop scheduling tasks. Schedule when your brain actually works.' [Show energy curve visualization] (11-15s) 'Then work in focused chunks instead of 8-hour marathons—that's it.' [Show 2-3 burst work sessions]. This sequences concepts instead of stacking them.

weaknesses.issue: CTA ('follow for the full system') lacks differentiation—competitor accounts use identical language, so no reason to follow *this* account over others promising the same.
weaknesses.fix: Rewrite CTA (15-17s): 'Follow—I'm showing you the exact 3-step template I use with 200+ students who actually stick to their schedules.' [On-screen: '@[handle]' + subtle social proof]. Specificity (template + numbers) signals authority over vague 'system' promise.

weaknesses.issue: Shareability blocked by lack of pattern-interrupt or surprising insight—video explains problem+solution competently but doesn't create 'aha' moment that makes someone tag a procrastinating friend.
weaknesses.fix: Add micro-surprise at 9-sec mark: After 'schedule energy,' show quick cut of someone successfully working (satisfied expression) with text: 'This student went from 3 reschedules/week to 0 in 2 weeks.' [Pause 1s]. This social proof + contrast creates share trigger ('that could be me') without adding length.

captions: your schedule isn't the problem. you are—just kidding, your brain is. your brain ≠ a spreadsheet. stop fighting it. swipe for the 3-step template that actually works →

schedules fail because you're not lazy, you're just planning wrong. here's what i teach: energy beats time, backwards deadlines beat deadlines, and chunks beat marathons. follow for the full breakdown →
growth.final_call_reason: Strong hook and audience fit (8-9 range), but middle section cognitive overload and weak CTA differentiation need tightening before posting—resequence value propositions and add social proof to unlock higher shareability (currently 6, should be 8+).
